subject: english-language
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the assessment objectives.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: A travel article says "You will love every breathtaking moment of this paradise." What is its main PURPOSE?
options: To persuade the reader to visit
questions.explain: Positive, emotive language directed at "you" is designed to persuade the reader to go.

questions.q: Identifying a writer's VIEWPOINT means working out:
options: Their attitude or opinion towards the subject
questions.explain: Viewpoint is the writer's stance or attitude on the topic.

questions.q: An extract opens with a long, calm description of a sunny garden, then a single line: "Then the screaming began." What is the structural effect of this shift?
options: It signals the end of the story
It tells us the setting is unimportant
It creates a jarring contrast that shocks the reader
questions.explain: The sudden shift from calm to violence creates contrast and shock, a deliberate structural effect.

questions.q: Words like "buzz," "crash" and "hiss" that imitate sounds are examples of:
questions.explain: Words that sound like what they describe are onomatopoeia.

questions.q: "His coat was patched and his shoes had holes, but he held his head high." What does this most strongly imply about the character?
questions.explain: The contrast between worn clothes and a high-held head implies pride and dignity despite hardship.

questions.q: "Her smile was as bright as the sun." This is an example of a:
questions.explain: A comparison using "as" is a simile.

questions.q: "The snake slid silently across the soft sand." The repeated soft "s" sound is:
questions.explain: Repetition of "s"/soft hissing sounds is sibilance.

questions.q: "The wind whispered through the trees." Which technique is this?
questions.explain: Giving the wind the human ability to "whisper" is personification.

questions.q: A writer's TONE in "Honestly, what a complete and utter shambles this has become" is best described as:
questions.explain: The dismissive phrasing conveys scorn and frustration.

questions.q: A short, abrupt sentence such as "He ran." placed among long ones is used to:
questions.explain: A short sentence among longer ones creates emphasis and impact.

questions.q: A writer describes a character who "forced a thin smile and changed the subject quickly." What can you most reasonably INFER?
options: The character has just woken up
The character is about to tell a long story
The character is uncomfortable and wants to avoid the topic
The character is feeling genuinely cheerful
questions.explain: A forced smile and a quick subject-change imply discomfort and avoidance rather than the explicit emotion of happiness.
Repeated initial "s" sounds in "silent slippery snakes slid" is alliteration.
